title: How SF's most powerful mom became a political force
author: Ezra Wallach
summary: Ezra Wallach's profile traces how Meredith Dodson turned pandemic-era parent frustration into SF Parents, an advocacy organization that grew from a Facebook group into a $1.2 million political force reshaping San Francisco school board elections and district policy. The piece is candid about the organization's trajectory: founded to demand school reopening and address learning loss among disadvantaged students, it became powerful enough to swing a board election by fewer than 300 votes and to be credited — or blamed — for protecting Superintendent Maria Su from scrutiny. Wallach lets both admirers and critics speak, including a founding member who worries the group became 'part of the establishment' it once challenged. The reporting also holds Dodson's tenure up against hard outcomes: third-grade reading proficiency inched up to 49 percent but stayed below pre-pandemic levels, and racial achievement gaps widened even as the organization's influence grew. The profile closes on the succession to Rebecca Kee and Dodson's own ambivalence about whether her organization's hard-nosed politics ultimately served the children it was built to protect.
points: The revenue arc — from $18,000 in 2021 to over $1.2 million by 2024 — quantifies how quickly a grassroots pandemic-reopening group became a well-funded political operation capable of swinging a board election.

The 2024 board race, decided by fewer than 300 votes after SF Parents withheld support from moderate candidate John Jersin, is the clearest evidence in the piece that the organization's endorsements now carry decisive electoral weight.

The juxtaposition of Dodson's advocacy legacy against the district's actual outcomes — reading proficiency still below pre-pandemic levels and widening racial achievement gaps — complicates any simple narrative of her tenure as either triumph or overreach.
quotes: It developed substantial funding — revenue grew from $18,000 in 2021 to over $1.2 million by 2024, supported by foundations including Crankstart.
Critics, including some board members, view her as an unelected powerbroker who uses political leverage to protect Superintendent Maria Su and avoid challenging the administration.
The organization endorsed three of four 2024 board candidates while withholding support from moderate candidate John Jersin, who lost by fewer than 300 votes to progressive Matt Alexander.

Reading proficiency among third-graders reached 49% in 2026, up slightly from 47% but below pre-pandemic levels. Achievement gaps widened: approximately 19% of Black and 24% of Hispanic third-graders read proficiently versus 62% of Asian and 72% of white students.
One anonymous founding member noted the group had become "part of the establishment" and lost willingness to challenge uncomfortable issues.
Dodson described the work as exhausting — describing education politics as a "knife fight in a phone booth.
